Interested in how frontier labs pre-train image/video generation models?
We were too.

Since those recipes are rarely made public in full, we started from the most mature pretraining playbook available in the open: how modern LLMs are built.
Introducing Chimera: a visual generation model family that brings LLM-style hybrid linear attention and scaling co-design to visual generation.

In large-scale pretraining, nearly every design choice eventually shows up.
That means solving architecture design and scaling as one coupled problem: every architectural choice changes how the model scales, and scaling behavior determines which choices actually survive.
Chimera approaches both jointly, building a model family that remains predictable as model size, compute budget, and data distribution change.

Our key architectural observation is a simple division of labor: a single raster-ordered KDA stream carries long-range state, while modality-aware short convolutions preserve native local geometry.
Together, they form an effective and elegant linear-attention backbone for multidimensional visual data, with periodic MLA providing direct global interaction and sparse MoE expanding capacity at controlled activated compute.

This design comes with a useful effect: NoPE.
In Chimera, position is represented by the computation itself. KDA’s ordered recurrence and learned state decay encode order and recency, while the short convolutions encode local spatial-temporal structure.
Explicit positional embeddings are not needed in our design.
Because these mechanisms are not tied to a fixed training grid or sequence length, Chimera shows strong zero-shot extrapolation in both space and time.
Trained exclusively on 1K images and 5-second videos, it directly generates coherent 4K images with little visible quality degradation and 30-second videos with only 6.5% FID degradation over the final five seconds, all zero-shot, without resolution- or length-specific finetuning.

But architecture alone is not a pretraining recipe unless it scales predictably.
Thus, scaling should not be treated as an afterthought: fitting a curve over model sizes is easy; making that curve meaningful is much harder.
If every model size is differently under-tuned, your scaling law may simply be measuring optimization error.
We propose HeteroP to transfer proxy-tuned hyperparameters module by module across width and depth, giving us a consistently tuned model family. This allows us to fit Chinchilla-style laws over activated model size, training tokens, and the image-video data mixture.

The laws not only provide the reference for compute-optimal model and data size, but also suggest that visual generation may be more model-hungry than we tend to assume.
Under the same parametric loss-fitting method used in Chinchilla, compute-optimal model size grows as FLOPs^0.516 for images, compared with FLOPs^0.46 for language. Video is even more model-hungry, with the exponent rising from 0.516 for images to 0.544 for video.
Guided by these laws, we trained an 11B-parameter Chimera that activates only 2B parameters per token, using ~600 H100 days.
- It matches Wan-2.1 2B pretraining loss with 7.3x fewer FLOPs, and runs 2.14x faster than full attention at 255K tokens.
- It matches FLUX.1-dev and Z-Image-Turbo on GenEval and outperforms both on DPG-Bench, using roughly 20× less training compute than Z-Image-Turbo.

Ultimately, Chimera indicates that once you pretrain at scale, every decision shows up.
And if the Kimi K3 recipe caught your attention, Chimera may look oddly familiar, except the tokens are pixels and frames with diffusion models.

PrismaX: Building the Real Service Layer for Physical AI

Most people talking about “Physical AI” are still stuck at the demo stage. Cool robot videos, impressive lab results, big model announcements. But the hard truth is this: robots are hardware-rich and data-poor. The machines exist. The foundation models are getting better. What’s missing is enough high-quality, real-world data to teach them how to actually work outside perfect lab conditions.

PrismaX is attacking that exact bottleneck.

What they’re doing is straightforward but powerful. They run a live teleoperation platform where regular people can log in through a browser (https://t.co/W2Wlb4ewfX) and remotely control real robots — arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, and more. Every session generates valuable visual and action data. That data gets scored for quality, cleaned, and fed into training pipelines for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models.

They’re not just collecting random footage. They’re building a full closed loop:

1. Human operators control real hardware in real environments.
2. High-quality demonstrations are captured at scale.
3. A growing community of validators scores the data for usefulness (motion quality, semantic value, diversity, aesthetics).
4. The best data trains better models.
5. Better models make robots more capable, which creates demand for even better data.

The “Verify Quality” system that just went public is the first public piece of their VLA Foundry. Anyone can score robot training data and earn points. The top performers will become the First 100 — the founding data quality validators. This is how they plan to scale judgment beyond a small internal team to a large community.

Key strengths that actually matter:

- Real robots, not simulations. You’re controlling physical machines, not virtual ones. The data has the noise, friction, and unpredictability of the real world.
- Browser-based access. No special hardware or complex setup required on the operator side. Low barrier for humans to contribute.
- Multi-robot support. They already work across different form factors and manufacturers instead of locking into one platform.
- Quality-first approach. Data isn’t just volume — it’s filtered and scored so models train on what actually helps.
- Strong early backing. $11M seed led by a16z CSX, with participation from Stanford Blockchain Builder Fund, Symbolic, Volt Capital, Virtuals Protocol and others. The team (Bayley Wang & Chyna Qu) mixes robotics depth with crypto-native incentive design.
- Clear path from teleoperation → data flywheel → autonomy. Teleop isn’t the end goal. It’s the data engine that should eventually reduce the need for constant human control.

Physical AI doesn’t fail because of missing robots or missing models. It fails because of missing high-quality, diverse, real-world experience data at scale. PrismaX is one of the few teams treating that data problem as the core product, not a side effect.

They’re building the service layer that sits between humans, robots, and intelligence — and they’re doing it with actual machines running and a community already scoring the results.

If you want to see what real physical AI infrastructure looks like in practice, go to https://t.co/9SlpeuAB3m and try Live Control or start validating data. The gap between digital intelligence and physical capability is still wide. Projects that close it with real operations and real data will matter more than the ones that just talk about it.

RLHF by hand ✍️ ~ 15 steps walkthrough below

Train a model on human text and it inherits human bias. It will assume a doctor is a "him", because the data says so.

RLHF is the correction. A human marks one preference, doc is them over doc is him, and the weights move.

But one correction is not the point. The hope is that the model learns the value behind it, gender neutrality, and applies it to professions nobody ever mentioned.

How does it work?

Goal: train a reward model from a single human comparison about doctors, then turn it on CEOs, filling in every cell yourself.

= 1. Given =

A reward model, an LLM, and two (prompt, next) pairs.

= 2. Preferences =

A human reads both pairs and picks a winner: (doc is, them) beats (doc is, him). The loser is not bad grammar, it is gender bias, and that is the whole signal.

= 3. Word embeddings =

Let us look up each word of the loser pair. These vectors are the reward model's input.

= 4. Linear layer =

We multiply by the reward model's weights and add its biases. Out come feature vectors, one per position.

= 5. Mean pool =

Let us multiply by [1/3, 1/3, 1/3], which averages the three positions into one sentence embedding.

= 6. Output layer =

We map that sentence down to a single number. Reward = 3.

= 7. The winner, the same way =

Let us repeat steps 3 to 6 on the winning pair. Reward = 5.

= 8. Winner minus loser =

We take the gap: 5 - 3 = 2. The reward model wants this positive and as large as it can make it.

= 9. Loss gradient =

Let us squash the gap into a probability, σ(2) ≈ 0.9, and subtract the target of 1. The gradient is -0.1, and it goes back through the purple weights. The reward model is now trained.

= 10. A prompt it has never seen =

We start the second half with "[S] CEO is". The feedback in step 2 was about doctors. Nothing connects a CEO to a doctor except what the reward model generalised.

= 11. Transformer =

Let us push it through attention and a feed forward layer, one vector per position.

= 12. Output probabilities =

We map each vector to a score over the vocabulary.

= 13. Sample =

Let us take the highest score. The model completes "CEO is" with "him", which is the same bias the human penalised in step 2.

= 14. Score it with the reward model =

We feed the new pair (CEO is, him) through steps 3 to 6. Reward = 3, exactly the score it gave "doc is him" in step 6. Nobody taught it about CEOs. The value transferred.

= 15. Loss gradient =

Let us set the loss to the negative of the reward, so minimising the loss maximises the reward. The gradient is a constant -1, and it goes back through the red weights.

The outputs:
Loser reward = 3, winner reward = 5
Reward gap = 2, predicted σ ≈ 0.9, reward model gradient = -0.1
LLM samples "him", reward = 3, LLM gradient = -1

Congrats! You just calculated RLHF by hand.

And you watched a value generalise: one comparison about doctors, and the model marks down "CEO is him" unprompted.

MiniMax H3 video model opens a path around closed AI video vendors

MiniMax open-sourced H3, a multimodal video model it calls "Seedance-level." It takes up to 9 images, 3 video clips, and 3 audio tracks, 12 files max, and turns them into finished-feeling spots. APPSO testers gave it seven screenshots and a one-sentence prompt and got a promo video. A fictional fashion spot came out looking close to a real ad.

The stronger capability is editing. H3 can swap a background, replace an object, change a character's outfit, or shift the camera angle while keeping the original motion and look. It topped Artificial Analysis's global video editing leaderboard at launch, ahead of Gemini Omni. That is the pain point most video generation models skip: making a first version is easy, revising it is not.

Our read: open source matters more than the benchmark. We have argued before that ByteDance's Seedance wins on distribution. MiniMax is taking a different route, letting teams host the model and build their own production workflow instead of paying for tokens and staying tied to a vendor's cost structure.

A 20-YEAR-OLD GUY FROM USA CREATED AN AI COSPLAY MODEL AND 826 MEN PAID TO FOLLOW HER

Investment: $140 for AI video generation
Subscription price: $11.99
Total revenue: $9,904

The idea wasn't to create another generic AI influencer. Instead, he built a recognizable cosplay character with a polished visual identity, combining anime-inspired fashion, energetic dance videos and a confident on-camera personality that immediately stood out in short-form feeds

To attract attention, he consistently uploaded short lip-sync and dance clips on TikTok, using eye-catching costumes and trending audio to maximize reach. As the audience grew, viewers were directed to Fanvue, where subscribers could access exclusive content and interact directly with the AI persona

Project became profitable after just 38 days, while the original investment was earned back within the first two weeks, showing how a strong visual concept and consistent content can turn a small AI experiment into a subscription business
